title: Fermat's Two-Square Theorem
statement: A prime p is expressible as p = a² + b² (integers a, b) if and only if p = 2 or p ≡ 1 (mod 4). Equivalently, prime p is NOT a sum of two squares if and only if p ≡ 3 (mod 4).
overview: Fermat conjectured this result in 1640 and Euler gave the first complete proof in 1749. The key insight is that whether a prime splits, stays inert, or ramifies in the Gaussian integers ℤ[i] determines exactly whether it is a sum of two squares. The proof uses two main ingredients: (1) squares mod 4 are only 0 or 1, so a²+b² cannot be ≡ 3 (mod 4), giving the impossibility direction; (2) Mathlib's `Nat.Prime.sq_add_sq` (from the Gaussian integer theory) gives existence when p ≢ 3 (mod 4).
openQuestion: Fermat's two-square theorem follows directly: p is a sum of two squares iff p = 2, p ≡ 1 (mod 4).
keyResults: fermat_two_squares_prime: full biconditional p prime is sum of two squares ↔ p=2 or p%4=1
fermat_two_squares_3mod4: primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) are never sums of two squares
fermat_two_squares_1mod4: primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) are always sums of two squares
Non-examples: 3, 7, 11, 19 (≡3 mod 4) proved not to be sums of two squares
historicalContext: Fermat stated this theorem in a letter to Mersenne in December 1640 without proof. Euler proved it in 1749 after 7 years of effort. The modern proof via Gaussian integers (ℤ[i]) was given by Dedekind. The key insight is that primes ≡ 1 (mod 4) split in ℤ[i] while primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) are inert.
